latin.336: Phantasia quoque & appetitus sensitivus eam distinctionem non norunt. Quod si ut facultas agat propter finem ultimum, oportet distinctionem finis ultimi a subordinatis illam facultatem nosse, necesse etiam erit ut eandem distinctionem cognitam habeat facultas quae tendit in finem subordinatum ultimum: itaque nulla, ut dixi, hominis facultas, praeter unam mentem aget propter finem. Idem de universa natura, quam propter finem agere, a Philosophis demonstrari solet. Nihil igitur falsius illa viri docti propositione. Porro cum homo mente & voluntate tendit in verum ultimum finem, eodem etiam omnia hominis tendant, & ab eo referuntur: at cum a vero fine ultimo aberrat, ab eodem etiam fine eius omnes aberrant facultates. Quis autem nescit quam libidine proclivis sit ad facultate generandi abutendum ad voluptatem? Et quando illa tributa est a Deo ac destinata ad procreationem similis, posita in generante universali corruptione, fieri non potest quin, non Dei, sed corrupti generantis vitio, generet corruptum, sicut facultas genitrix leprosi generat leprosum: determinatur enim eam ad rem non ab autore naturae, sed a depravatione eius cuius est facultas.
latin.337: GAR. Deinde cum finem ultimum vir doctus proponat, qui in veri finis locum successerit, falso apparentem, nempe fallacem felicitatis speciem in creaturis reperiendam, quomodo statim desilit ad generationem, hoc est, a generali fine ad singularem? Non enim qui agnoscit successisse, in locum veri finis ultimi finem alium falso apparentem, ideo statim concludere cogitur, eum finem esse debere generationem. Cur enim potius quam scientiam, vel voluptatem, vel bona externa, &c. nisi aliunde pateat ratio, quare potius successisse dicatur in locum veri finis ultimi generatio, quam aliud quodlibet?
latin.338: PLAC. Ludere mihi potius videtur vir doctus his verbis, & sequentibus, quam serio argumentari. Nonne enim fallax illa felicitatis species multis in rebus quaeritur? At cur non potius voluptatem dixi quam generationem? nempe quia coitus voluptatem sic visum est honeste significare id quod miror aut non animadvertisse virum doctum, aut, si animadvertit, dissimulasse. Quis enim quaeso concupiscentiae carnalis & libidinis est scopus? gloria Dei? aedificatio proximi? certe nihil nisi fallacem sequitur felicitatis & voluptatis umbram. id quod in iis cernere est qui huiusmodi concupiscentiis laxant fraena: aliud enim nihil quaerunt quam cupitis potiri, & libidinem explere. Itaque quae vir doctus subiungit, non videntur mihi ulla egere responsione.
latin.339: GAR. Sed fac omnia haud aliter habere, quam quomodo viro docto libuit: vim generatricem esse facultatem moralem; corruptionem Adami convertisse ad generationem tanquam finem ultimum, eodem conversam fuisse totam partem superiorem animae cum appetitu sensitivo, id est, totum Adamum; ex iis promanasse corruptum semen. Haec omnia tamen non effecerint, ut corruptio illa prima prognatos ex Adamo inquinet, nisi aliud aliquid adjungatur. Nam & idem in aliis accidere potest. Homo se periuriis, adulteriis, homicidiis, &c. contaminabit, & pessimos habitus inde contrahet: vim genitricem suam, appetitum sensitivum, & partem animae superiorem, & se totum, quantus quantus est, ad generationem convertet, tanquam finem ultimum: tamen, ultra sua illa, quibus justam condemnationem in caput suum accersivit, propagatione naturali non derivabit in posteros, sicut Adamo factum. Aliud ergo quippiam intercessisse necesse est in primo illo peccato, quod in aliis patrum peccatis non ita habet. Nimirum Deus, cui ius est absolutum in creaturas suas, primum illud Adami peccatum justissimo judicio imputatum voluit omnibus ipsius posteris: aliorum peccata non ita vult in omnes posteros descendere.
latin.340: PLAC. Quo sensu facultas genitrix a me dicatur aliquatenus moralis, jam exposui, nimirum ratione concupiscentiae seu libidinis, & destinationis ad procreandum morum subjectum. Patet etiam quo sensu dixerim eam conversam fuisse ad actum generandi tanquam ad ultimum finem, nempe quia aliud non spectat libido quam voluptatem: Eatenus etiam corrupta a me dicitur, quatenus non solum ad propagationem facultatum hominis tendit, sed etiam ad propaganda corruptionem, in quo scopo, cuius gratia creata fuit, recedit. Hac immunditie posita necessario sequitur prognatos ex Adamo inquinari. At cur idem non accidit in aliis peccatis? quia alia peccata non induxerunt in parentes universalem corruptionem, sed ex ea profecta sunt, nihilque addiderunt praeter universalis illius corruptionis particulares quasdam determinationes ad quaerendam foelicitatem potius in tali re quam in alia, tali voluptate quam in aliqua alia, itaque mirum videri non debet si corruptio universalis propagatur, non propagantur particulares determinationes seu habitus.
latin.341: Est enim, nostra quidem sententia, universalis illa corruptio posita in propensione ad falsum finem ultimum, & aversione a vero fine. Est enim appetitus finis ultimi necessarius, quia primo omnium appetitur. itaque creari hominem oportuit cum appetitu veri finis, & nunc nasci necesse est cum appetitu finis falso apparentis, si non actu, saltem propensione, ob inductam in naturam nostram per lapsum Adami finis ultimi mutationem: quae mutatio per perjuria, adulteria, & homicidia non fit, itaque non propagantur. Hinc est quod particulares eiusmodi habitus seu determinationes aliquomodo corrigi & mutari possunt, & non raro ab uno vitio in oppositum flectimur: Sed universalis illa corruptio nisi per gratiam regenerationis auferri a nobis nequit. Quod si haec nostra non placet responsio, malim saltem dicere, huius discriminis hanc esse causam, quod noluerit Deus impedire quominus primum illud Adami peccatum propagaretur, alia vero eius & aliorum patrum peccata, quominus etiam ipsa propagarentur, voluerit impedire. Hoc enim satius videtur quam imputationem antecedentem comminisci, quae tamen non obstat, quin ad Dei voluntatem discrimen illud totum referendum sit. Caeterum hic mihi videntur conjungi duo non satis bene coherentia, cum imputatio illa Adamici peccati fieri a Deo dicitur pro absoluto suo in creaturas iure, & tamen justissimo judicio.

pass_a.336: Placeus presses the mind-only tip from GAR's faculty-versus-user split. Phantasy and sensitive appetite also lack knowledge of last versus subordinate ends; if that knowledge is required for a faculty to act for a last end, then only the mind acts for an end—and philosophers even say universal nature acts for ends—so GAR's proposition is false. When man by mind and will aims at the true last end, all his faculties tend with him; when he wanders from it, they all wander. Lust is prone to abuse the generative faculty for pleasure; once universal corruption sits in the begetter, that faculty begets corrupt as a leper's generative faculty begets a leper, determined by the owner's depravation rather than by Nature's Author.
pass_a.337: GAR next asks why, once Placeus posits a falsely apparent last end—a fallacious species of happiness found in creatures—he at once leaps from that general end to generation as the singular stand-in. Acknowledging some false successor to the true last end does not compel the conclusion that the successor must be generation. Why not science, or pleasure, or external goods, unless some further reason shows why generation rather than any other should be said to have taken the true last end's place?
pass_a.338: Placeus answers that GAR seems to play with words rather than argue in earnest. That fallacious happiness-species is sought in many things; he said generation rather than bare pleasure because naming the pleasure of coitus was the honest way to signify what he meant—which GAR either missed or dissembled. Carnal concupiscence and lust aim neither at God's glory nor the neighbor's edification, but only at a fallacious shade of happiness and pleasure, plain in those who loosen the reins and seek only to obtain desires and fill lust. What GAR subjoins needs no reply.
pass_a.339: GAR grants for argument Placeus's whole chain: generative power as moral faculty; Adam's corruption turned to generation as last end; whole superior soul with sensitive appetite—the whole Adam—turned likewise; corrupt seed flowing from these. Still that would not stain those born of Adam unless something else is added. Other men may contaminate themselves with perjury, adultery, murder, contract worst habits, and turn generative power and whole self to generation as last end, yet not by natural propagation derive that into posterity as Adam did. So something intervened in the first sin that other fathers' sins lack: God, with absolute right over creatures, willed by most just judgment that Adam's first sin be imputed to all his posterity, and does not so will other sins to descend.
pass_a.340: Placeus recalls in what sense the generative faculty is somehow moral: by concupiscence or lust, and by destination to procreating a moral subject. It was turned to generating as last end because lust looks at nothing but pleasure; it is corrupted insofar as it tends not only to propagate man's faculties but also to propagate corruption, leaving the purpose for which it was created. That uncleanness set, Adam's offspring are necessarily stained. Other sins do not do the same, because they did not induce universal corruption in parents but proceeded from it and added only particular determinations of where to seek happiness—so universal corruption propagates, particular habits do not.
pass_a.341: In Placeus's judgment universal corruption is a propensity to a false last end and aversion from the true. Appetite of a last end is necessary and first; man was created with appetite of the true end and now is born with appetite of a falsely apparent end, at least in propensity, by the last-end change Adam's fall induced. Perjury, adultery, and murder do not make that change, so they are not propagated; particular habits can be corrected and even bent to opposites, but only regenerating grace removes the universal. Prefer that reply to inventing antecedent imputation, though the discrimination still refers to God's will. Tip: absolute right over creatures and most just judgment seem badly joined in the imputation claim.

336: Phantasy too and the sensitive appetite do not know that distinction. But if for a faculty to act for a last end it must know the distinction of the last end from the subordinate ones, then the faculty that tends to a subordinate last end must also have that same distinction known: and so, as I said, no faculty of man except the mind alone will act for an end. The same of universal nature, which the Philosophers are accustomed to prove acts for an end. Nothing therefore is falser than that proposition of the learned man. Further, when a man by mind and will tends to the true last end, all that is his tends the same way and is referred from it; but when he wanders from the true last end, all his faculties wander from that same end. Who does not know how prone lust is to abuse the generative faculty for pleasure? And when that faculty was given by God and destined to the procreation of a like, once universal corruption is set in the begetter, it cannot but be—not by God's fault but by the vice of the corrupt begetter—that it begets the corrupt, just as the generative faculty of a leper begets a leper: for it is determined to that thing not by the author of nature, but by the depravation of him whose faculty it is.
337: GAR. Next, when the learned man proposes a last end which has succeeded into the place of the true end, falsely apparent—namely a fallacious species of happiness to be found in creatures—how does he at once leap to generation, that is, from a general end to a singular one? For he who acknowledges that another falsely apparent end has succeeded into the place of the true last end is not therefore at once compelled to conclude that that end must be generation. Why rather than science, or pleasure, or external goods, &c., unless a reason appear from elsewhere why generation rather than any other whatever should be said to have succeeded into the place of the true last end?
338: PLAC. The learned man seems to me to play with these words and what follows, rather than to argue in earnest. For is not that fallacious species of happiness sought in many things? But why did I not rather say pleasure than generation? Namely because by the pleasure of coitus it seemed honest to signify that which I marvel either that the learned man did not notice, or, if he noticed, that he dissembled. For what, I ask, is the aim of carnal concupiscence and lust? the glory of God? the edification of the neighbor? Certainly it follows nothing but a fallacious shade of happiness and pleasure—which is plain in those who loosen the reins to such concupiscences: for they seek nothing else than to obtain what they desire and to satisfy lust. And so what the learned man adds does not seem to me to need any reply.
339: GAR. But grant that all stand no otherwise than as it pleased the learned man: that the generative power is a moral faculty; that Adam's corruption turned it to generation as a last end; that the whole superior part of the soul with the sensitive appetite—that is, the whole Adam—was turned the same way; that corrupt seed flowed from these. Still all this would not have brought it about that that first corruption should stain those born of Adam, unless something else be added. For the same can happen in others. A man will contaminate himself with perjuries, adulteries, murders, &c., and will contract the worst habits from them; he will turn his generative power, sensitive appetite, and superior part of soul, and himself entire as much as he is, to generation as a last end: yet beyond those things by which he has drawn just condemnation on his own head, he will not by natural propagation derive it into posterity as was done in Adam. Something else therefore must have intervened in that first sin which does not so hold in other sins of fathers. Namely God, who has absolute right over his creatures, willed by most just judgment that that first sin of Adam be imputed to all his posterity: he does not so will other sins to descend upon all posterity.
340: PLAC. In what sense the generative faculty is called by me somehow moral, I have already set out—namely by reason of concupiscence or lust, and of destination to procreating a moral subject. It is also plain in what sense I said it was turned to the act of generating as to a last end—namely because lust looks at nothing but pleasure. So far also it is called by me corrupted, insofar as it tends not only to the propagation of man's faculties, but also to propagating corruption, in which it recedes from the purpose for which it was created. That uncleanness being set, it necessarily follows that those born of Adam are stained. But why does the same not happen in other sins? Because other sins did not bring universal corruption into the parents, but proceeded from it, and added nothing except certain particular determinations of that universal corruption toward seeking happiness rather in this thing than in that, in such a pleasure than in some other: and so it ought not to seem strange if universal corruption is propagated, while particular determinations or habits are not.
341: For that universal corruption is, in our judgment, set in a propensity to a false last end and an aversion from the true end. For the appetite of a last end is necessary, because it is appetited first of all. And so man had to be created with an appetite of the true end, and now must be born with an appetite of a falsely apparent end, if not in act at least in propensity, because of the change of last end induced into our nature by Adam's fall: which change is not made by perjuries, adulteries, and murders, and so those are not propagated. Hence such particular habits or determinations can somehow be corrected and changed, and not rarely we are bent from one vice to the opposite: but that universal corruption cannot be taken from us except by the grace of regeneration. But if this our reply does not please, I would rather at least say that the cause of this discrimination is that God was unwilling to hinder that first sin of Adam from being propagated, but was willing to hinder his other sins and those of other fathers from being propagated also. For this seems better than to invent an antecedent imputation—which nevertheless does not prevent that whole discrimination from being referred to God's will. For the rest, two things not well coherent seem here to be joined, when that imputation of Adam's sin is said to be done by God by his absolute right over creatures, and yet by most just judgment.
